correctness.rationale: Checked density-matrix positivity |c|^2<=p(1-p), Gaussian characteristic-function channel multiplication and normalized output Wigner polynomial. Completing the square yields a negative disk iff 2 eta p/A+|c|^2/p>1; if A>=2 eta this cannot hold for any input, whereas every pure p>0 state has a disk when A<2 eta. For fixed p in (0,1) any mixed coherence can be written as a strict convex mixture of opposite-coherence pure states. Their disks differ on positive-area subsets, making the negative-part convexity strict. For pure states, shifting the negative disk gives convolution of the radially decreasing Gaussian with a centered radially decreasing positive paraboloid; layer-cake disk intersection shows it is strictly maximized at zero shift (p=1), so N

value.rationale: Integrated Wigner negative volume is a natural optical nonclassicality resource for experimentally realizable vacuum/one-photon inputs subject to thermal attenuation. Determining optimal output resource under a fixed mean-photon excitation constraint and over the complete mixed Bloch ball is a motivated exact invariant and channel capacity, not simply demonstrating negativity of one prepared state. The strict pure-state equality class and Fock global optimizer are useful for constrained preparation and thermal-loss benchmarking.

final_claim: For all mixed/pure optical vacuum–one-photon inputs passed through a phase-insensitive thermal attenuator, Wigner negativity vanishes iff A>=2 eta for the universal capacity, otherwise its unique global maximizer is the one-photon Fock state with maximum (2 eta/A) exp(-1+A/(2 eta)) - 1; at fixed excitation p in (0,1), exactly pure vacuum–one-photon superpositions maximize negative volume, with an exact Bessel-integral optimum and strict upper bound N
limitations: Single mode and Fock levels 0,1 only, phase-insensitive thermal attenuation, no heralding or squeezing.
Unique maximization requires A<2eta; at A>=2eta every state has zero negative volume.
Exact one-dimensional Bessel formula not generally elementary; grid/quadrature tests are not proofs.
